cadmaPy.overview:
Overview

CADMA Py is a graphical interface for the CADMA-Chem protocol (Computer-Assisted Design of Multifunctional Antioxidants based on Chemical properties). It is intended to:

  • Compare pharmacokinetic-relevant properties between a reference set and one or more sets of proposed molecules.
  • Combine ADME, toxicity and synthetic accessibility into a single selection score \(S_S\) that can be used as a first filter.
  • Build or update disease-specific reference sets that serve as normalization anchors for future projects.

The software does not replace detailed pharmacokinetic modelling, full QSAR development or expert medicinal chemistry judgement. It provides a transparent scoring layer to triage large lists of drug-like molecules consistently.

The CADMA-Chem protocol in three stages

Stage 1 — Reference set. Define the disease or therapeutic problem. Build a curated list of oral drugs used for that indication, with experimental or predicted ADMETSA data. Compute mean and standard deviation for all properties.

Stage 2 — First-pass screening (where CADMA Py is focused). Design or import candidates (SMILES). Predict ADME descriptors, toxicity and SA. Normalise each property with respect to the reference set. Compute multiparametric scores and rank candidates.

Stage 3 — Refinement. For the most promising candidates, perform detailed quantum chemistry, pKa and speciation analysis, passive transport estimations, docking, similarity indices, and retrosynthetic planning.
cadmaPy.workflow:
Workflow

CADMA Py implements the Stage 2 — first-pass screening of the CADMA-Chem protocol. The wizard guides you through four steps. The full protocol diagram (Stages 1–3) is available from the 📊 Protocol diagram button.

Step 1 — Select a reference family

Choose a pre-built disease baseline (Neuro for neurological drugs, RETT for Rett syndrome) or create a custom family from your own SMILES, toxicity and SA data.

The reference set provides the mean and standard deviation for every property — these are the normalisation anchors for all scores.

Step 2 — Import candidates

Upload molecular data through one of three routes:

  • Smile-it: combinatorial SMILES generation.
  • Toxicity + SA jobs: predictions from the ADMET apps already available in this platform.
  • CSV upload: bulk import with column mapping.

Step 3 — Configure the formula

Adjust ADME interval windows and component weights for your specific screening needs. Every parameter has sensible defaults derived from classical drug-likeness rules.

Step 4 — Review results

Inspect the ranked candidates table, score histograms and per-metric plots. The global selection score \(S_S\) combines ADME, toxicity and synthetic accessibility. Export the full report as CSV.
cadmaPy.adme-intervals:
ADME interval window

The ADME intervals in CADMA-Chem derive from classical medicinal chemistry rules for oral drug-likeness. Each rule proposes acceptable physicochemical limits; CADMA-Chem adopts the restrictive overlap of these ranges to create a clear, practical filter for early screening.

Origin of CADMA-Chem intervals

Additional heuristics

  • CNS polarity window: TPSA ≤ 60–70 Å², MW ≤ 400, logP ~2–4 → favours CNS penetration.
  • Pfizer 3/75: logP > 3 and TPSA < 75 Å² → higher toxicity risk from excessive permeability.
  • Pfizer 2/100: HBD ≤ 2 and TPSA < 100 Å² → good probability of oral absorption.
  • GSK 4/400: logP ≤ 4 and MW ≤ 400 → reduced clinical failure probability from toxicity.
  • Teague lead optimisation: early leads: MW 100–350, logP 1–3 — leaves room for growth during optimisation.
  • Brenk structural alerts: identifies reactive substructures that may compromise safety.

Each physicochemical metric has a configurable interval window (min–max). A candidate passes a metric when its value falls inside the band.

cadmaPy.adme-properties:
ADME properties

CADMA Py relies on RDKit to compute a panel of physicochemical descriptors for every molecule. These form the ADME dimension of the selection score.

Descriptor calculation

MWMolecular WeightDescriptors.MolWt

HBLAH-Bond Acceptors (Lipinski)CalcNumLipinskiHBA
HBLDH-Bond Donors (Lipinski)CalcNumLipinskiHBD
RBRotatable BondsCalcNumRotatableBonds
PSATopological Polar Surface AreaCalcTPSA

MMutagenicity / Ames (0–1)TEST prediction
LD50Oral rat LD50 (mg/kg)TEST prediction
SASynthetic AccessibilityAMBIT / BRSA / RDKit

Per-metric alignment score

For each metric the reference family supplies a mean and standard deviation. The binary flag for each property is:

$$ \mathrm{ADME}_P(i) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } P_{\min} \leq P(i) \leq P_{\max} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$

The aggregate ADME score is:

$$ S_{\mathrm{ADME}}(i) = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{P} \mathrm{ADME}_P(i)} {\Sigma_{\mathrm{ADME,ref}}} $$

where \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{ADME,ref}}\) is the number of ADME properties that the reference set itself satisfies within the same intervals. By construction, \(S_{\mathrm{ADME}}\) grows when more properties fall inside the desired ADME window.
cadmaPy.reference-sets:
Reference sets

A reference set is a curated collection of drugs that define the desired ADMETSA behaviour for a given disease. CADMA Py uses them to compute mean and standard deviation of all properties, which serve as normalisation anchors for selection scores.

Included seed families

SetMean MWMean logPMean LD50 (mg/kg)Mean SA
Neuro291.312.551131.3774.07
RETT289.772.221751.0476.98
  • Neuro — approved drugs for neurological conditions (epilepsy, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, etc.)
  • RETT — compounds relevant to Rett syndrome and related developmental disorders

Required input files for custom families

To build a new reference set you need:

  1. SMILES file — containing name and smile columns.
  2. Toxicity CSVs — from EPA TEST: DT, M (Ames), LD50.
  3. Synthetic accessibility CSV — SA index from AMBIT (scale 1–100).

Processing pipeline

Internally, CADMA Py reads and sanitises the SMILES, computes ADME descriptors with RDKit, merges toxicity and SA tables using molecule names as keys, computes averages and standard deviations, and stores these statistics persistently for future sessions.
cadmaPy.selection-scores:
Selection scores

CADMA Py combines ADME, toxicity and synthetic accessibility into a set of scalar scores. All formulas are explicit so every ranking can be traced back to the original data.

Toxicity sub-scores

LD50 alignment (higher LD50 → less toxic → rewarded):

$$ S_{\mathrm{LD50}}(i) = 1 + \log_{10}\left( \frac{1 + \mathrm{LD50}(i)} {1 + \overline{\mathrm{LD50}}_{\mathrm{ref}}} \right) $$

Mutagenicity and developmental toxicity (lower values → less toxic → rewarded):

$$ S_M(i) = 1 - \log_{10}\left( \frac{1 + M(i)}{1 + \overline{M}_{\mathrm{ref}}} \right) \qquad S_{\mathrm{DT}}(i) = 1 - \log_{10}\left( \frac{1 + \mathrm{DT}(i)}{1 + \overline{\mathrm{DT}}_{\mathrm{ref}}} \right) $$

The "+1" shift avoids taking the logarithm of zero for very small predicted values.

Overall toxicity score (arithmetic mean of the three):

$$ S_T(i) = \frac{S_{\mathrm{LD50}}(i) + S_M(i) + S_{\mathrm{DT}}(i)}{3} $$

ADME–toxicity combined score

$$ S_{\mathrm{ADMET}}(i) = S_{\mathrm{ADME}}(i) + S_T(i) $$

Synthetic accessibility score

$$ S_{\mathrm{SA}}(i) = \frac{\mathrm{SA}(i)}{\overline{\mathrm{SA}}_{\mathrm{ref}}} $$

\(S_{\mathrm{SA}} > 1\) indicates the derivative is easier to synthesise than the reference drugs. Higher SA values mean easier synthesis on the AMBIT scale.

Global selection score \(S_S\)

The three blocks are combined with fixed weights:

$$ S_S(i) = \underbrace{0.4 \cdot S_{\mathrm{ADME}}(i)}_{\text{ADME weight}} + \underbrace{0.4 \cdot S_T(i)}_{\text{Toxicity weight}} + \underbrace{0.2 \cdot S_{\mathrm{SA}}(i)}_{\text{SA weight}} $$

Interpretation: \(S_S = 1\) is the reference threshold — the derivative is, on average, as "good" as the reference drugs. \(S_S > 1\) indicates global improvement. Results are sorted from highest to lowest \(S_S\).

Reference formula values

MetricSymbolDefault reference
LD50LD50_ref450 mg/kg
MutagenicityM_ref0.12
Dev. ToxicityDT_ref0.20
SA ScoreSA_ref84

Default references are the averages of the selected reference family. All values are overridable in the formula controls.
cadmaPy.conformers:
Conformers from SMILES

CADMA Py can generate 3D conformers for selected molecules and export them as SDF files for quantum chemistry, docking or other 3D-based workflows.

Input modes

  1. From a selection-score CSV: load a \(S_S\) CSV, pick the top-N molecules by score, and generate their 3D structures.
  2. From a manual SMILES list: paste SMILES strings (one per line). Invalid entries are discarded automatically.

Conformer count by flexibility

Rotatable Bonds (RB)Conformers generated
≤ 210
3 – 520
6 – 830
9 – 1250
> 1275

Workflow

  1. SMILES → MolFromSmiles
  2. Add explicit hydrogens (AddHs)
  3. Generate \(N\) conformers using ETKDGv3
  4. Optimise with UFF force field
  5. Select the lowest-energy conformer → SDF export

The SDF output contains optimised 3D coordinates, compound name, selection score and other properties as SD tags, ready for external tools (Gaussian, ORCA, AutoDock, etc.).

Note: Generated conformers are starting points — they lack solvent effects and electronic-level optimisation. Re-optimisation with DFT or other appropriate methods is essential before final energy calculations or docking.

easyRate.overview:
Easy-rate: TST + Eckart rate constants

This app computes kinetic rate constants for chemical reactions using Transition State Theory (TST) with optional Eckart tunnelling and diffusion corrections. It reads thermochemical data directly from Gaussian log files.

Required inputs

Five Gaussian log files must be provided:

  • Reactant 1 and Reactant 2: optimised geometries with thermochemical analysis (freq).
  • Transition state: one imaginary frequency.
  • Product 1 and Product 2 (at least one) — optimised product geometries.

Processing pipeline

  1. Parse Gaussian logs: extract SCF energy, thermal enthalpy, Gibbs free energy, ZPE, temperature, imaginary frequency.
  2. Compute thermodynamic deltas: \(\Delta H\), \(\Delta G\), \(\Delta ZPE\) for both reaction and activation.
  3. Apply cage-effect correction (optional) to the activation Gibbs energy.
  4. Compute Eckart tunnelling correction \(\kappa_{TST}\) from the TS imaginary frequency and barrier/reaction energies.
  5. Compute the TST rate constant with path degeneracy.
  6. Apply diffusion correction (optional) using Stokes–Einstein theory.
easyRate.formulas:
TST rate constant:

$$ k_{TST} = \sigma \cdot \kappa_{TST} \cdot \frac{k_B T}{h} \cdot \exp\left(\frac{-\Delta G^{\ddagger}}{RT}\right) $$

where \(\sigma\) is the reaction path degeneracy, \(\kappa_{TST}\) the Eckart tunnelling factor, \(k_B T/h\) the fundamental frequency factor (\(\approx 2.08 \times 10^{10} \, T\) s⁻¹), and \(\Delta G^{\ddagger}\) the Gibbs free energy of activation.

Eckart tunnelling correction:

$$ u = \frac{h c \tilde{\nu}}{k_B T}, \quad \alpha_1 = \frac{2 \pi \Delta V_f^{\ddagger}}{h c \tilde{\nu}}, \quad \alpha_2 = \frac{2 \pi (\Delta V_f^{\ddagger} - \Delta_r E)}{h c \tilde{\nu}} $$ $$ \kappa_{TST} = \frac{G^*}{\exp(-u)} $$

Diffusion correction:

If enabled, the observed rate constant is:

$$ k_{obs} = \frac{k_{diff} \cdot k_{TST}}{k_{diff} + k_{TST}} $$

where \(k_{diff} = 4 \pi N_A D_{AB} R\) is the Stokes–Einstein diffusion-controlled rate, \(D_{AB} = D_A + D_B\) the mutual diffusion coefficient, and \(R\) the encounter distance.

Cage effect:

When cage effects are enabled, the activation Gibbs energy is reduced by:

$$ \Delta G^{\ddagger}_{cage} = \Delta G^{\ddagger} - RT \ln(N_r \cdot 10^{2N_r - 2}) + (N_r - 1) $$

where \(N_r\) is the number of reactant molecules.

marcus.overview:
Marcus electron transfer theory

This app computes electron transfer rate constants according to the Marcus theory (Marcus, 1956–1965). It reads thermochemical data from Gaussian log files to calculate the adiabatic and vertical energies, the reorganisation energy (\(\lambda\)), and the resulting Marcus barrier and rate constant.

Required files (6 Gaussian logs)

  • Reactant 1 and Reactant 2: optimised ground-state geometries.
  • Product 1 (adiabatic) and Product 2 (adiabatic): relaxed product geometries (full optimisation).
  • Product 1 (vertical) and Product 2 (vertical): single-point energies at the reactant geometry (or vice-versa) to compute the vertical reorganisation.

Physical picture

Marcus theory describes electron transfer as a thermally activated process where the nuclear coordinates must reorganise before the electron can tunnel from donor to acceptor. The reorganisation energy \(\lambda\) is the energy required to distort the nuclear framework from the equilibrium geometry of the reactants to that of the products without transferring the electron.
marcus.formulas:
Adiabatic energy:

$$ \Delta E_{adj} = E_{SCF}^{P1_{adj}} + E_{SCF}^{P2_{adj}} - E_{SCF}^{R1} - E_{SCF}^{R2} $$

Thermally corrected adiabatic energy:

$$ \Delta G_{adj} = G^{P1_{adj}} + G^{P2_{adj}} - G^{R1} - G^{R2} $$

Vertical energy:

$$ \Delta E_{vert} = E_{SCF}^{P1_{vert}} + E_{SCF}^{P2_{vert}} - E_{SCF}^{R1} - E_{SCF}^{R2} $$

Reorganisation energy:

$$ \lambda = \Delta E_{vert} - \Delta G_{adj} $$

Marcus activation barrier:

$$ \Delta G^{\ddagger} = \frac{\lambda}{4} \left(1 + \frac{\Delta G_{adj}}{\lambda}\right)^2 $$

Rate constant:

$$ k_{ET} = \frac{k_B T}{h} \cdot \exp\left(\frac{-\Delta G^{\ddagger}}{RT}\right) $$

Diffusion correction (optional):

$$ k_{obs} = \frac{k_{diff} \cdot k_{ET}}{k_{diff} + k_{ET}} $$

References

molarFractions.overview:
Molar fractions: acid-base speciation

This app computes the speciation diagram (molar fraction vs. pH) for a polyprotic acid or base. Given a set of \(pK_a\) values and an initial charge for the fully protonated species, it calculates the fraction of every protonation state across a range of pH values.

The underlying model is the standard mass-balance / Henderson–Hasselbalch formalism for coupled acid-base equilibria. At any pH the fractions of all species sum to 1.0 (conservation of mass).

Key concepts

  • Speciation: the distribution of a compound among its protonation states as a function of pH.
  • Polyprotic system: a molecule with \(n\) ionisable groups has \(n+1\) species (fully protonated → fully deprotonated).
  • \(pK_a\): the pH at which two adjacent species are at equal concentration.
  • Initial charge: charge of the fully protonated form (e.g. +1 for ammonium, 0 for neutral acid).

Typical use cases

  • Predicting the dominant species at physiological pH (7.4) for drug-like molecules.
  • Understanding pH-dependent solubility, permeability and reactivity.
  • Designing buffers and analysing titration curves.
molarFractions.algorithm:
Algorithm

1. Cumulative beta coefficients

Starting from \(\beta_0 = 1\), each successive formation constant is:

$$ \beta_k = 10^{\sum_{j=1}^{k} K_{n-j+1}} $$

where \(K_j\) are the acid dissociation constants (pKa values) in the user-defined order.

2. Species fraction at a given pH

The hydrogen ion concentration is \([H^+] = 10^{-pH}\). The fraction of species \(i\) (which has lost \(i\) protons relative to the fully protonated form) is:

$$ f_i = \frac{\beta_i \cdot [H^+]^{i}}{\sum_{j=0}^{n} \beta_j \cdot [H^+]^{j}} $$

3. Species labelling

Labels follow the convention: \(H_n A q\) for the fully protonated species, where \(n\) is the number of pKa values and \(q\) is the initial charge. Each deprotonation removes one \(H^+\) and reduces the charge by one.

4. Numerical grid

  • pH values are generated from \(pH_{min}\) to \(pH_{max}\) with step \(\Delta pH\).
  • Minimum step: 0.05
  • Grid size: 8 – 350 points
  • pKa values: 1 – 6

References

saScore.overview:
Synthetic Accessibility Score

The Synthetic Accessibility (SA) Score estimates how easy or difficult it is to synthesise a given molecule in a laboratory. It is used as a practical filter in drug-discovery pipelines to deprioritise molecules that are theoretically interesting but prohibitively difficult to synthesise.

Score scale

All methods report scores on a 0–100 scale after conversion:

  • 100: very easy to synthesise (highly accessible)
  • 0: extremely difficult to synthesise

The conversion from the classic 1–10 (RDKit) scale is:

$$ SA_{0-100} = 100 - \frac{(SA_{1-10} - 1) \times 100}{9} $$
saScore.methods:
Available methods

AMBIT

Uses the AMBIT Java library to predict SA scores from fragment-based analysis. The score is calculated by evaluating the complexity and frequency of structural fragments against a reference database of known synthetic compounds.

BR-SAScore (BRSAScore)

A vendorised RDKit implementation using pre-computed fragment contributions. BR-SA extends the original RDKit SA score with additional fragment libraries and re-calibrated contributions for improved accuracy on drug-like molecules.

RDKit SA Score

The classic implementation from rdkit.Contrib.SA_Score.sascorer. It decomposes a molecule into fragments and compares their frequency against the PubChem database. Rare fragments → high score (difficult synthesis). The original score (1–10) is converted to the 0–100 scale.

Which method to choose?

  • AMBIT: good for general-purpose screening with a large training set.
  • BR-SAScore: improved accuracy for medicinal-chemistry-oriented molecules.
  • RDKit: fastest, most established baseline; well-documented.

Multiple methods can be selected simultaneously for cross-validation.

smileit.overview:
Smile-it: combinatorial SMILES generation

Smile-it is a combinatorial SMILES generator that takes a core molecular scaffold (represented as a SMILES string) and systematically attaches chemical substituents at user-defined positions.

Core concept

The approach follows the classical medicinal-chemistry strategy of scaffold decoration: a central core is functionalised with diverse substituents to create a focused library of analogues. Smile-it automates this process combinatorially, ensuring chemically valid structures through RDKit-based valence and bond-order checks.

Applications

  • Generating virtual libraries for virtual screening.
  • Exploring substituent space around a hit compound.
  • Preparing inputs for ADME, toxicity and synthetic accessibility predictions (CADMA Py pipeline).
  • R-group decomposition and SAR (structure–activity relationship) exploration.
smileit.workflow:
Workflow

1. Input the scaffold

Draw or paste the core molecule in SMILES notation. Smile-it canonicalises the SMILES and inspects the structure to show atoms, properties and structural pattern annotations.

2. Select substitution sites

Click on atoms in the molecular viewer to mark them as substitution sites. Up to 20 sites can be selected.

3. Define assignment blocks

Each block maps a set of substituents to a set of sites:

  • Choose substituents from the catalog (persistent entries) or add manual SMILES.
  • Assign substituent categories (aromatic, H-bond donor, hydrophobic, etc.) as filters.
  • Blocks can overlap on the same site; overlapping is resolved by priority (last-block-wins).

4. Configure generation

  • R-substitutes: number of iterative substitution rounds (1–10).
  • Max structures: soft limit to prevent combinatorial explosion (0 = unlimited).
  • Export name: base name for derivative numbering.

5. Generate and export

The engine performs iterative rounds of RDKit-based fusion, checking chemical validity at each step. Results include SMILES, SVG previews, traceability (which substituent went where), and exportable CSV/ZIP bundles.
smileit.algorithm:
Generation algorithm

Iterative substitution

In Round 1, the engine finds all valid embeddings of the principal scaffold, then attempts to fuse each substituent at each selected site. Valid derivatives become frontier nodes for Round 2.

In Round 2+, each existing derivative serves as a new starting point. Substituents are applied to the sites still available (sites left free in that derivative's traceability chain).

RDKit fusion

Each fusion attempt chemically joins the substituent to the scaffold site using RDKit's MolFromSmiles and custom valence-aware bond formation. Invalid combinations (e.g. exceeding valence limits) are rejected.

Deduplication and caching

  • Duplicate SMILES are discarded at each round.
  • A fusion-attempt cache prevents re-computing the same (scaffold, substituent, site) combination across different branches.
  • If \(max\_structures\) is set, generation stops once the limit is reached (truncated flag raised).

Traceability

Each generated structure retains a full audit trail of which substituent (from which block) was attached to which site in which round, enabling full reproducibility.

toxicityProperties.overview:
Toxicity Properties with ADMET-AI

This app predicts key toxicological properties for a list of molecules using the ADMET-AI machine learning platform. For each molecule it computes acute toxicity (LD50), mutagenicity (Ames test) and developmental toxicity (DevTox).

ADMET-AI

ADMET-AI (Swanson et al., 2024) is a deep-learning model trained on large-scale experimental ADMET datasets. It provides fast, high-throughput predictions suitable for screening large chemical libraries prior to experimental testing.

Predicted end-points

  • LD50 (acute toxicity): median lethal dose in mg/kg (oral, rat). Higher values indicate lower acute toxicity.
  • Ames mutagenicity: probability (0–1) that the compound is mutagenic. Classified as Positive ≥ 0.5.
  • Developmental toxicity (DevTox): probability (0–1) of developmental toxicity risk. Classified as Positive ≥ 0.7.
toxicityProperties.interpretation:
Interpretation of results

LD50 (mg/kg)

LD50 range (mg/kg)Toxicity classification
≤ 5Super toxic
5 – 50Extremely toxic
50 – 500Highly toxic
500 – 5000Moderately toxic
> 5000Practically non-toxic

The LD50 is log-transformed by ADMET-AI and converted back to mg/kg using the molecular weight. Higher LD50 values are generally preferred in drug discovery.

Ames mutagenicity

  • Score ≥ 0.5: Positive (mutagenic — potential safety concern)
  • Score < 0.5: Negative (non-mutagenic)

Developmental toxicity

  • Score ≥ 0.7: Positive (developmental toxicity risk)
  • Score < 0.7: Negative (low risk)

The thresholds (0.5 for Ames, 0.7 for DevTox) follow the ADMET-AI recommended operating points and are consistent with the original publication.

tunnel.overview:
Eckart tunneling correction

This app computes the quantum tunneling correction factor \(\kappa_{TST}\) for chemical reaction rate constants using an asymmetric Eckart potential barrier.

In Transition State Theory (TST) the classical rate constant is multiplied by \(\kappa_{TST}\) to account for quantum-mechanical tunnelling through the reaction barrier. The Eckart model provides an analytical potential that approximates the true barrier shape using the forward barrier height, the reaction energy and the imaginary frequency at the transition state.

Asymmetric Eckart barrier

The asymmetric Eckart potential \(V(x)\) is defined by three parameters: \(\alpha_1\), \(\alpha_2\) and \(u\). The tunnelling probability \(G(E)\) is integrated numerically over the barrier using a 40-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature to yield \(G^*\), the integrated transmission coefficient.

Physical meaning

  • \(\kappa_{TST} > 1\): the reaction is faster than classical TST predicts, indicating significant tunnelling.
  • Larger \(\kappa_{TST}\) values are typical for H-atom transfer reactions and low-temperature kinetics.
  • Imaginary frequency: the curvature at the transition state (higher → sharper barrier → more tunnelling).
tunnel.formulas:
Reduced barrier frequency:

$$ u = \frac{h \cdot c \cdot \tilde{\nu}}{k_B \cdot T} $$

where \(h\) is Planck's constant, \(c\) the speed of light, \(\tilde{\nu}\) the imaginary frequency (cm⁻¹), \(k_B\) Boltzmann's constant and \(T\) the temperature.

Barrier shape parameters:

$$ \alpha_1 = \frac{2 \pi \cdot \Delta V_f^{\ddagger}}{h \cdot c \cdot \tilde{\nu}} $$ $$ \alpha_2 = \frac{2 \pi \cdot (\Delta V_f^{\ddagger} - \Delta_r E)}{h \cdot c \cdot \tilde{\nu}} $$

where \(\Delta V_f^{\ddagger}\) is the forward barrier (ZPE-corrected) and \(\Delta_r E\) is the reaction energy (ZPE-corrected).

Integrated transmission coefficient:

The tunnelling probability \(G(E)\) is integrated over the barrier energy range:

$$ G^* = \int_{E_{min}}^{E_{max}} G(E) \, dE $$

Tunnelling correction factor:

$$ \kappa_{TST} = \frac{G^*}{\exp(-u)} $$

The denominator \(\exp(-u)\) is the classical Boltzmann transmission factor. \(\kappa_{TST}\) is the ratio of the quantum to the classical transmission.
tunnel.references:
References

  • Eckart, C. Phys. Rev. 1930, 35, 1303. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.35.1303
  • Cramer, C. J. Essentials of Computational Chemistry, 2nd ed.; Wiley, 2004.
  • Fernández-Ramos, A.; Ellingson, B. A.; Meana-Pañeda, R.; et al. J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2007, 3, 1797. DOI: 10.1021/ct700092m
